_note: Year 3 Term 2 Maths item bank (Australian Curriculum v9.0): 16 skills x 10 items covering place value, time, multiplication, money, mental strategies, 3D shapes, mass/capacity, data and graphing, fractions, chance, fact families, choosing units, estimation, and grid references.

items.questionText: Work out 245 + 138.
stepByStepSolution: Add the ones: 5 + 8 = 13, so write 3 and carry 1 ten.
Add the tens: 4 + 3 + 1 (carried) = 8.
Add the hundreds: 2 + 1 = 3, giving 383.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to carry the extra ten after adding the ones.
Adding the digits in the wrong column (e.g. mixing up tens and hundreds).
hints: Line up the ones, tens and hundreds columns first.
Start with the ones column: 5 + 8, and remember to carry.

items.questionText: Work out 500 - 267.
stepByStepSolution: Since there are 0 tens and 0 ones in 500, regroup a hundred into 10 tens, and a ten into 10 ones.
Subtract the ones: 10 - 7 = 3. Subtract the tens: 9 - 6 = 3.
Subtract the hundreds: 4 - 2 = 2, giving 233.
commonMisconceptions: Trying to subtract 7 from 0 without regrouping first.
Regrouping only one place value when two are needed.
hints: You can't take 7 away from 0, so you'll need to regroup.
Think of 500 as 4 hundreds, 9 tens and 10 ones.

items.questionText: What is 1,000 more than 2,345?
stepByStepSolution: Look at the thousands digit in 2,345, which is 2.
Add 1 to the thousands digit: 2 + 1 = 3.
Keep the other digits the same, giving 3,345.
commonMisconceptions: Adding 1,000 to the wrong place value column.
Changing more digits than just the thousands digit.
hints: Only the thousands digit needs to change.
2 thousands plus 1 more thousand is how many thousands?

stepByStepSolution: Add the ones: 7 + 5 = 12, write 2 and carry 1.
Add the tens and hundreds, carrying each time it's needed: 6+4+1=11 (write 1, carry 1), 3+8+1=12 (write 2, carry 1).
Add the thousands: 1+2+1=4, giving 4,212.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to carry across more than one column.
Losing track of a carried digit partway through.
hints: Work from the ones column and carry any extra ten each time.
Write the carried digits above the next column so you don't forget them.

stepByStepSolution: Regroup to subtract the ones: 3 becomes 13 after borrowing from the tens.
Continue regrouping across the tens, hundreds and thousands as needed.
Subtract each column carefully to get 2,745.
commonMisconceptions: Stopping regrouping after only one column when several are needed.
Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger digit regardless of position.
hints: You'll need to regroup more than once because of the zero in the tens place.
Think of 6,203 as 6 thousands, 1 hundred, 9 tens and 13 ones.

items.questionText: The Lightning Ridge library has 4,250 books. On Tuesday, 1,876 books were borrowed. How many books are still in the library?
stepByStepSolution: This is a subtraction problem: 4,250 - 1,876.
Regroup across the columns as needed and subtract carefully.
The answer is 2,374 books still in the library.
commonMisconceptions: Adding the numbers instead of subtracting.
Making a regrouping error partway through the subtraction.
hints: Think about whether the number of books goes up or down.
Set up 4,250 - 1,876 in columns and regroup where needed.

items.questionText: Which number sentence shows the correct regrouping when working out 532 - 268? A) 5 hundreds, 3 tens, 2 ones becomes 4 hundreds, 12 tens, 2 ones   B) 5 hundreds, 3 tens, 2 ones becomes 4 hundreds, 2 tens, 12 ones   C) 5 hundreds, 3 tens, 2 ones stays the same
items.answerKey: 5 hundreds, 3 tens, 2 ones becomes 4 hundreds, 2 tens, 12 ones
stepByStepSolution: To subtract 8 from 2 in the ones place, you need to regroup a ten into 10 ones.
This changes 3 tens into 2 tens, and 2 ones into 12 ones.
The hundreds stay at 5 until you check if more regrouping is needed elsewhere.
commonMisconceptions: Regrouping a hundred instead of a ten by mistake.
Thinking no regrouping is needed because 532 looks bigger than 268 overall.
hints: Look closely at just the ones column: can you take 8 away from 2?
Borrowing a ten turns 3 tens and 2 ones into 2 tens and 12 ones.

stepByStepSolution: Line up the digits by place value: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones.
Subtract each column from right to left: 9-7=2, 9-6=3, 9-5=4, 9-4=5.
No regrouping is needed here since every digit on top is bigger, giving 5,432.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming regrouping is always needed, even when it isn't.
Subtracting the top digit from the bottom digit instead of the other way around.
hints: Check each column: is the top digit always bigger than the bottom digit here?
Subtract straight down each column from the ones to the thousands.

items.questionText: A charity raised $3,678 in week one and $2,945 in week two, then spent $1,200 on new sports equipment. How much money did the charity have left?
stepByStepSolution: First add the two weeks together: 3,678 + 2,945 = 6,623.
Then subtract the amount spent: 6,623 - 1,200.
This gives 5,423 left over.
commonMisconceptions: Only using one of the two weeks' amounts instead of adding both.
Subtracting before adding, which changes the order of the steps.
hints: This is a two-step problem: first combine, then take away.
Add the two weekly amounts first, then subtract the $1,200.

items.questionText: Maya says 7,000 - 3,254 = 4,246. Is she correct? A) Yes, that is correct   B) No, the correct answer is 3,746   C) No, the correct answer is 4,746
stepByStepSolution: Work out 7,000 - 3,254 carefully by regrouping across the zeros.
7,000 becomes 6 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens and 10 ones for the subtraction.
Subtracting column by column gives 3,746, so Maya's answer is not correct.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming an answer must be right just because it looks close.
Making a regrouping mistake when there are several zeros in a row.
hints: Try working out the subtraction yourself before deciding if Maya is right.
Regrouping across zeros can be tricky — take it one column at a time.

items.questionText: How many minutes are in 1 hour?
stepByStepSolution: Think about a clock face and how the minute hand moves.
The minute hand goes all the way around once every hour.
There are 60 minutes in 1 hour.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing minutes in an hour with seconds in a minute.
Guessing 100 because it feels like a round number.
hints: Think about how a clock is divided into small marks.
Count how many minute marks are on a clock face.

items.questionText: How many seconds are in 1 minute?
stepByStepSolution: Think about counting slowly: '1 Mississippi, 2 Mississippi...' up to a minute.
A minute is made up of 60 of these seconds.
So there are 60 seconds in 1 minute.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up seconds and minutes because they sound similar.
Guessing a smaller number like 10 or 30.
hints: This is the same number as minutes in an hour!
Count how many seconds tick by on a clock during one minute.

items.questionText: How many hours are in 1 day?
stepByStepSolution: Think about a full day and night together.
A clock shows 12 hours twice each day (once for day, once for night).
12 + 12 = 24 hours in a day.
commonMisconceptions: Only counting daylight hours instead of the whole day and night.
Guessing 12 because a clock face only shows up to 12.
hints: Think about both the daytime and the night-time.
A clock goes around twice in a full day.

items.questionText: Which activity would most likely take about 5 minutes? A) Brushing your teeth   B) Watching a whole movie   C) Sleeping overnight
stepByStepSolution: Think about how long each activity usually takes in real life.
Watching a movie takes much longer than 5 minutes, and sleeping overnight takes hours.
Brushing your teeth is a short task that fits best with about 5 minutes.
commonMisconceptions: Choosing an activity based on how important it feels rather than how long it takes.
Not comparing all three options before deciding.
hints: Picture yourself doing each activity — which one finishes quickly?
A movie and a night's sleep both take far more than a few minutes.

items.questionText: It takes Ben 45 minutes to walk to his grandma's house. It takes Priya 1 hour to walk to hers. Who takes longer, and by how many minutes?
stepByStepSolution: Change 1 hour into minutes: 1 hour = 60 minutes.
Compare 60 minutes (Priya) with 45 minutes (Ben).
Priya takes longer, by 60 - 45 = 15 minutes.
commonMisconceptions: Comparing 1 hour and 45 minutes without converting them to the same unit first.
Subtracting the wrong way round and getting a negative idea of the difference.
hints: Change the hour into minutes so you're comparing the same units.
Once both times are in minutes, subtract to find the difference.

items.questionText: A school lunch break lasts 40 minutes. If it starts at 12:00, what time does it finish?
stepByStepSolution: Start at 12:00 and count on in minutes.
Add 40 minutes to 12:00.
This gives a finish time of 12:40.
commonMisconceptions: Adding 40 minutes and accidentally moving into the next hour.
Confusing the start time with the finish time.
hints: Count on from 12:00 in your head or on a clock face.
12:00 plus 40 minutes is still before 1 o'clock.

items.questionText: Is the statement true or false? 2 hours is the same length of time as 90 minutes. A) True   B) False
stepByStepSolution: Change 2 hours into minutes: 2 x 60 = 120 minutes.
Compare 120 minutes with 90 minutes.
They are not equal, so the statement is False.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 2 hours equals 100 minutes instead of 120.
Not converting hours to minutes before comparing.
hints: Work out how many minutes are in 2 hours first.
2 hours is more than 90 minutes.

items.questionText: A movie starts at 3:15 and finishes at 5:00. How many minutes long is the movie?
stepByStepSolution: From 3:15 to 4:15 is exactly 1 hour, which is 60 minutes.
From 4:15 to 5:00 is 45 more minutes.
Add the two parts together: 60 + 45 = 105 minutes.
commonMisconceptions: Only counting the hour part and forgetting the extra 45 minutes.
Subtracting the times directly without lining up the minutes correctly.
hints: Break the time into an easy chunk of one full hour first.
Work out 3:15 to 4:15, then add on the rest of the time to 5:00.

items.questionText: Sione's swimming lesson goes for 50 minutes. If it starts at 4:40, at what time does it finish?
stepByStepSolution: From 4:40, count on 20 minutes to reach 5:00.
That leaves 50 - 20 = 30 minutes still to add.
5:00 plus 30 more minutes gives a finish time of 5:30.
commonMisconceptions: Adding all 50 minutes without noticing the hour changes partway through.
Miscounting how many minutes are left after reaching 5:00.
hints: Try counting on to the next hour mark first (5:00), then add what's left.
How many minutes are left over after you reach 5:00?

items.questionText: Which is the best estimate for how long it takes to eat a bowl of cereal? A) About 5 minutes   B) About 5 hours   C) About 5 seconds
stepByStepSolution: Think about how long breakfast usually takes in real life.
5 seconds is far too fast, and 5 hours is far too long for a bowl of cereal.
About 5 minutes is the most sensible estimate.
commonMisconceptions: Choosing an extreme option without thinking about realistic timing.
Confusing minutes with hours when estimating everyday tasks.
hints: Picture yourself actually eating breakfast — is it over in seconds, or does it take longer?
Compare the three options to a real, everyday amount of time.

items.questionText: Break 23 into tens and ones. What are they?
stepByStepSolution: Look at the tens digit in 23, which is 2, meaning 2 tens (20).
Look at the ones digit in 23, which is 3, meaning 3 ones.
So 23 is made up of 20 and 3.
commonMisconceptions: Splitting the number into the wrong place values, such as 2 and 3.
Forgetting that the tens digit stands for a multiple of ten, not just '2'.
hints: The first digit tells you how many tens there are.
2 tens is the same as the number 20.

items.questionText: Use partitioning to work out 12 x 3. (Hint: 12 = 10 + 2)
stepByStepSolution: Split 12 into 10 and 2.
Multiply each part by 3: 10 x 3 = 30, and 2 x 3 = 6.
Add the parts together: 30 + 6 = 36.
commonMisconceptions: Only multiplying one of the two parts by 3.
Adding 10 and 2 before multiplying instead of after.
hints: Multiply 10 x 3 first, then work out 2 x 3.
Add your two answers together at the end.

items.questionText: What is 10 x 14?
stepByStepSolution: Multiplying by 10 means adding a zero to the end of the number.
14 with a zero added becomes 140.
commonMisconceptions: Adding two zeros instead of one when multiplying by 10.
Confusing multiplying by 10 with multiplying by 100.
hints: Multiplying by 10 is a quick pattern — what happens to the digits?
Just add one zero to the end of 14.

items.questionText: Use an area model to work out 23 x 14. First find 20 x 14. What is 20 x 14?
stepByStepSolution: 20 x 14 is the same as 2 x 14, then multiplied by 10.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to multiply by the extra 10 after working out 2 x 14.
Multiplying 20 x 14 as if it were 2 x 1.4.
hints: Break 20 into 2 tens to make the multiplication easier.
Work out 2 x 14 first, then multiply that answer by 10.

items.questionText: Using the area model for 23 x 14, find 3 x 14.
stepByStepSolution: Multiply 3 by 10 first: 3 x 10 = 30.
Multiply 3 by 4: 3 x 4 = 12.
Add the two parts: 30 + 12 = 42.
commonMisconceptions: Multiplying 3 by only one digit of 14 instead of both.
Adding instead of multiplying when combining the parts.
hints: Split 14 into 10 and 4 to make it easier.
Work out 3 x 10 and 3 x 4 separately, then add them.

items.questionText: Work out 23 x 14 by adding the parts: 20 x 14 = 280 and 3 x 14 = 42. What is 23 x 14 altogether?
stepByStepSolution: Take the two parts already found: 280 and 42.
Add them together: 280 + 42.
This gives a total of 322.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to add both parts together at the end.
Making an addition mistake when combining 280 and 42.
hints: You already have both parts of the area model — just combine them.
Add 280 and 42 carefully, lining up the place values.

items.questionText: Which is the correct way to split 32 x 15 using partitioning? A) (30 x 15) + (2 x 15)   B) (32 x 10) + (32 x 15)   C) (30 + 2) + (10 + 5)
stepByStepSolution: Partitioning means splitting one number into easier parts, like tens and ones.
32 can be split into 30 and 2, and each part is multiplied by 15.
This matches option A: (30 x 15) + (2 x 15).
commonMisconceptions: Splitting both numbers and then multiplying them together incorrectly.
Adding the parts instead of multiplying them first.
hints: Only one of the two numbers needs to be split into tens and ones.
Look for the option that splits 32, not 15.

items.questionText: Work out 34 x 12 using an area model or partitioning. Show your final answer.
stepByStepSolution: Split 34 into 30 and 4.
Multiply each part by 12: 30 x 12 = 360, and 4 x 12 = 48.
Add the parts together: 360 + 48 = 408.
commonMisconceptions: Adding the parts before finishing both multiplications.
Making a small addition error when combining 360 and 48.
hints: Split 34 into 30 and 4 to make the multiplication manageable.
Work out 30 x 12 and 4 x 12 separately, then add them together.

items.questionText: Work out 21 x 25 using partitioning.
stepByStepSolution: Split 21 into 20 and 1.
Multiply each part by 25: 20 x 25 = 500, and 1 x 25 = 25.
Add the parts together: 500 + 25 = 525.
commonMisconceptions: Splitting 25 instead of 21, which can make the numbers harder to work with.
Forgetting the '1 x 25' part completely.
hints: Splitting the smaller number (21) often makes this easier.
Work out 20 x 25 first, then add on 1 x 25.

items.questionText: Each box holds 24 party favours. There are 13 boxes. How many party favours are there in total?
stepByStepSolution: Split 13 into 10 and 3.
Multiply each part by 24: 10 x 24 = 240, and 3 x 24 = 72.
Add the parts together: 240 + 72 = 312.
commonMisconceptions: Adding 24 and 13 instead of multiplying them.
Losing track of one part of the partitioning when adding at the end.
hints: This is a multiplication word problem — think about equal groups.
Split 13 into 10 and 3 to make the multiplication easier.

items.questionText: How many cents are in $1?
stepByStepSolution: Think about the coins that make up one dollar.
There are 100 small parts, called cents, in every dollar.
So $1 is equal to 100 cents.
commonMisconceptions: Guessing 10 cents because of a mix-up with place value words.
Confusing cents with dollars when reading amounts.
hints: Think about how many 1 cent parts make up a dollar coin's value.
The answer is a number you'll use again and again with money.

items.questionText: Write $2.50 as cents.
stepByStepSolution: $2.00 is the same as 200 cents.
50 cents is already in cents.
Add them together: 200 + 50 = 250 cents.
commonMisconceptions: Writing 25 cents by only using the digits after the decimal point.
Forgetting to convert the whole dollar part into cents.
hints: Change the dollars into cents first, then add the extra cents.
$2 is 200 cents, plus another 50 cents.

items.questionText: Write 75 cents using the dollar sign and decimal point.
stepByStepSolution: 75 cents is less than one whole dollar.
Write a 0 before the decimal point to show there are no whole dollars.
Then write .75 for the cents, giving $0.75.
commonMisconceptions: Writing it as $75 instead of $0.75.
Leaving out the 0 before the decimal point.
hints: Since 75 cents is less than a dollar, the dollar part should be 0.
Remember to put a 0 before the decimal point.

items.questionText: Which amount is written correctly? A) $3.5.0   B) $3.50   C) 3$50
stepByStepSolution: Money amounts are written with a dollar sign first, then digits, then a decimal point with two digits for cents.
Option A has two decimal points, and option C has the dollar sign in the wrong place.
Only option B, $3.50, follows the correct format.
commonMisconceptions: Placing the dollar sign after the number instead of before it.
Using more than one decimal point in a money amount.
hints: A correctly written amount has one dollar sign and one decimal point.
Check where the dollar sign should go and how many digits follow the decimal point.

items.questionText: Write 340 cents as dollars and cents.
stepByStepSolution: 100 cents makes $1, so work out how many whole dollars are in 340 cents.
340 cents = 3 dollars (300 cents) with 40 cents left over.
Write this as $3.40.
commonMisconceptions: Writing $34.0 by misplacing the decimal point.
Forgetting the leftover cents after finding the whole dollars.
hints: Work out how many full 100s are in 340 first.
300 cents is $3, so what happens to the remaining 40 cents?

items.questionText: Which is worth more, $4.05 or $4.50? A) $4.05   B) $4.50   C) They are the same
stepByStepSolution: Both amounts have 4 whole dollars, so compare the cents.
$4.05 has 5 cents, while $4.50 has 50 cents.
50 cents is more than 5 cents, so $4.50 is worth more.
commonMisconceptions: Comparing the digits after the decimal point as if they were whole numbers without thinking about place value.
Assuming $4.05 is bigger because the 5 comes right after the point.
hints: Compare the cents parts carefully — line up the tens and ones.
Which is bigger: 5 cents or 50 cents?

items.questionText: Amelia has three $2 coins, one $1 coin, and one 50 cent coin. How much money does she have altogether?
stepByStepSolution: Three $2 coins make 3 x $2 = $6.
Add the $1 coin: $6 + $1 = $7.
Add the 50 cent coin: $7 + $0.50 = $7.50.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to include the 50 cent coin in the total.
Adding the coin values without lining up dollars and cents correctly.
hints: Add the dollar coins together first.
Then add on the smaller 50 cent coin at the end.

items.questionText: Write $12.05 in cents.
stepByStepSolution: $12.00 is the same as 1,200 cents.
5 cents is already in cents.
Add them together: 1,200 + 5 = 1,205 cents.
commonMisconceptions: Writing 125 cents by dropping the zero that shows there are no tens of cents.
Only converting part of the dollar amount into cents.
hints: Change the whole dollar amount into cents first.
Don't forget the zero that holds the tens-of-cents place.

items.questionText: Which list of amounts is ordered from smallest to largest? A) $2.05, $2.50, $2.55   B) $2.55, $2.50, $2.05   C) $2.50, $2.05, $2.55
stepByStepSolution: Compare the amounts by looking at the cents, since all have 2 whole dollars.
In cents: 5, 50, and 55 — order these from smallest to largest.
This gives $2.05, $2.50, $2.55, which matches option A.
commonMisconceptions: Ordering by the digit right after the decimal point instead of the whole cents value.
Assuming amounts with more digits are automatically bigger.
hints: Compare just the cents part of each amount.
5 cents, 50 cents and 55 cents — which order are these in from smallest?

items.questionText: Jordan is paying for a $6.75 lunch with a $10 note. Without working out the change yet, is $6.75 the same as 675 cents or 67.5 cents?
stepByStepSolution: $6.00 is the same as 600 cents.
75 cents is already in cents.
Add them together: 600 + 75 = 675 cents, not 67.5 cents.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the decimal point carries over directly into a decimal number of cents.
Forgetting to convert the whole dollars into cents before adding.
hints: Change the dollar part into cents first, then add the cents part.
Cents should always be a whole number, not a decimal.

items.questionText: Use doubling to work out 6 + 6.
stepByStepSolution: 6 + 6 is a double, so think of it as 2 groups of 6.
Doubling 6 means adding 6 to itself.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing doubling with adding one more instead of the same number again.
Miscounting when adding the two equal groups.
hints: Doubling means adding a number to itself.
What is 2 groups of 6?

items.questionText: What is 7 + 7?
stepByStepSolution: This is a double: 7 + 7.
Think of two equal groups of 7.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up 7 + 7 with 7 + 8 (a near double).
Losing count when adding the two sevens together.
hints: This is a doubles fact — you may already know it by heart.
Think of two hands with 7 fingers held up... nearly!

items.questionText: Bridge to 10 to work out 8 + 5. (Hint: 8 + 2 = 10, then...)
stepByStepSolution: Split 5 into 2 and 3, since 8 needs 2 more to make 10.
Add 8 + 2 to make 10.
Add on the remaining 3: 10 + 3 = 13.
commonMisconceptions: Splitting the wrong number, such as splitting 8 instead of 5.
Forgetting to add on the leftover part after reaching 10.
hints: Think about how many more 8 needs to reach 10.
Split 5 into two parts: one that makes 10 with 8, and what's left over.

items.questionText: Use a near double to work out 6 + 7. (Hint: think of 6 + 6, then add 1 more.)
stepByStepSolution: 6 + 6 is a double, which equals 12.
7 is one more than 6, so add 1 more to the double.
commonMisconceptions: Using the wrong double as the starting point, such as 7 + 7.
Forgetting to add the extra 1 after doubling.
hints: Find the nearest doubles fact to start from.
6 + 6 = 12, and 7 is just 1 more than 6.

items.questionText: Use bridging to 10 to work out 9 + 6.
stepByStepSolution: 9 needs just 1 more to make 10, so split 6 into 1 and 5.
Add 9 + 1 to make 10.
Add on the remaining 5: 10 + 5 = 15.
commonMisconceptions: Splitting 6 incorrectly so the parts don't add back up to 6.
Forgetting the leftover part after reaching 10.
hints: How many more does 9 need to reach 10?
Split 6 into that amount and what's left over.

items.questionText: Work out 15 - 8 using a mental strategy of your choice.
stepByStepSolution: Think of 15 as 10 + 5.
Take 8 away, perhaps by first taking away 5 to reach 10, then 3 more.
This leaves 7.
commonMisconceptions: Miscounting backwards by ones instead of using an efficient strategy.
Getting confused about which number to subtract from which.
hints: Try bridging back through 10.
15 take away 5 gets you to 10 — how much more do you still need to take away?

items.questionText: Which near-double strategy helps solve 8 + 9? A) Think of 8 + 8, then add 1   B) Think of 9 + 9, then subtract 2   C) Both A and B could work
items.answerKey: Both A and B could work
stepByStepSolution: 8 + 8 = 16, and adding 1 more gives 17.
9 + 9 = 18, and subtracting 2 also gives 16... let's check: 18 - 1 = 17, since 8 is 1 less than 9.
Both starting points can lead to the correct answer of 17 when adjusted correctly, so both strategies could work.
commonMisconceptions: Believing there is only one correct mental strategy for a given sum.
Adjusting the double by the wrong amount.
hints: There is often more than one good way to reach the same answer mentally.
Try both starting doubles and see if each one can be adjusted to work.

items.questionText: Use a mental strategy to work out 17 - 9.
stepByStepSolution: Think of 9 as close to 10.
Subtract 10 from 17 to get 7, since 9 is 1 less than 10.
Add back the 1: 7 + 1 = 8.
commonMisconceptions: Subtracting 10 and forgetting to add the 1 back on.
Counting backwards one at a time and losing track.
hints: Try rounding 9 up to 10 to make the subtraction easier.
Subtract 10 first, then adjust your answer by 1.

items.questionText: Use bridging to work out 14 + 7.
stepByStepSolution: 14 needs 6 more to make 20, so split 7 into 6 and 1.
Add 14 + 6 to make 20.
Add on the remaining 1: 20 + 1 = 21.
commonMisconceptions: Bridging to 10 instead of the nearest ten, 20, which makes the strategy less efficient.
Splitting 7 into parts that don't add back up to 7.
hints: Which multiple of 10 is closest to 14?
Split 7 so that one part takes 14 up to 20.

items.questionText: Explain which strategy you would use to solve 16 - 7 mentally, and give the answer.
stepByStepSolution: One strategy is to bridge back through 10: 16 - 6 = 10, then subtract the remaining 1.
commonMisconceptions: Losing track of how much has already been subtracted when splitting the number.
Choosing a strategy but not following through with all of its steps.
hints: Think about breaking 7 into two friendly parts.
16 take away 6 gets you to 10 — what's left to subtract?

items.questionText: How many faces does a cube have?
stepByStepSolution: Picture a cube, like a dice or a box.
Count each flat surface: top, bottom, and four sides.
A cube has 6 faces.
commonMisconceptions: Counting edges or vertices instead of faces.
Forgetting to count the top and bottom faces.
hints: A face is a flat surface you could trace with your finger.
Think of a dice — how many flat sides does it have?

items.questionText: How many vertices (corners) does a cube have?
stepByStepSolution: A vertex is a corner point where edges meet.
Picture a cube and count each pointy corner.
A cube has 8 vertices.
commonMisconceptions: Counting faces or edges instead of vertices.
Missing the corners that are on the bottom or hidden from view.
hints: A vertex is a sharp corner point, not a flat surface.
Try counting the corners on the top of a box, then the bottom.

items.questionText: Which 3D object has no flat faces at all? A) Cube   B) Sphere   C) Cone
stepByStepSolution: A cube has 6 flat faces, and a cone has one flat, circular face plus a curved surface.
A sphere, like a ball, is completely round with no flat surfaces anywhere.
This makes a sphere the object with no flat faces.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a cone has no flat faces because it looks round.
Confusing a sphere with a cylinder, which does have flat faces.
hints: Think about a ball versus a can versus an ice-cream cone.
Which of these three shapes is completely round all over?

items.questionText: How many edges does a cube have?
stepByStepSolution: An edge is a line where two faces meet.
A cube has 4 edges on the top, 4 on the bottom, and 4 connecting them.
commonMisconceptions: Counting faces or vertices instead of edges.
Only counting the edges that are easy to see and missing hidden ones.
hints: An edge is where two flat surfaces meet in a straight line.
Try counting the top square's edges, the bottom square's edges, and the ones joining them.

items.questionText: Which 3D object has exactly one curved face and one flat, circular face? A) Cone   B) Cylinder   C) Sphere
stepByStepSolution: A cylinder has two flat circular faces plus one curved face.
A sphere has no flat faces at all.
A cone has just one flat circular face and one curved surface, matching the description.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up a cone and a cylinder because both have circular parts.
Assuming any round object must be a sphere.
hints: Think about how many flat circles each shape has.
A cone comes to a point, unlike a cylinder.

items.questionText: A rectangular prism (like a tissue box) has how many faces?
stepByStepSolution: A rectangular prism has a top, bottom, front, back, and two sides.
Count each of these flat rectangular surfaces.
This gives a total of 6 faces.

items.questionText: Why is a tally useful when collecting this kind of data? A) It helps keep an accurate count while collecting answers one at a time   B) It automatically makes a graph   C) It removes the need to ask questions
items.answerKey: It helps keep an accurate count while collecting answers one at a time
stepByStepSolution: A tally is a simple way to record each answer as it is collected.
It does not create a graph by itself, and questions still need to be asked to gather the data.
Its real benefit is helping keep an accurate, running count, matching option A.
commonMisconceptions: Believing a tally automatically produces a finished graph.
Thinking data can be collected without asking any questions at all.
hints: Think about what a tally mark actually does when you're collecting answers.
Does it draw a graph, or does it just help you count?
